author: NewsBreak
title: How the 'Felony Lane Gang' Cashed In $16K in Broad Daylight at Adams County - NewsBreak
text: In what State Police are calling a textbook “Felony Lane Gang” scheme, authorities have charged 31‑year‑old Aireyonna Diamond Galicia of Baltimore with orchestrating a sophisticated identity‑theft ring that drained more than $16,800 from unsuspecting Adams County residents. Troopers say the case began on June 20, when a Butler Township woman parked outside the Gettysburg YMCA and left her purse in her unlocked car. Inside were her debit card, driver’s license and checkbook. “We’re all horrified this could happen in broad daylight,” said Troy Smith, manager at the Gettysburg YMCA, who reviewed bank surveillance stills with detectives. “It really shakes your sense of security in the community.” According to court charging documents, Galicia used the stolen items to forge and cash six fraudulent checks at drive‑through lanes of ACNB Bank branches on June 20 and 21, racking up $16,860 in illicit withdrawals. Detectives later uncovered a related loss of $2,500 from a second victim whose checkbook was also purloined, raising questions about whether more Adams County residents were targeted. Investigators credit the gang’s moniker—coined by ICE Homeland Security Investigations—for its use of the outermost bank lane, furthest from video cameras, to evade detection. Troopers say facial recognition software, combined with tattoo matches and social‑media sleuthing, decisively tied Galicia to the drive‑through transactions. The “Felony Lane Gang”—an organized theft ring based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida—has a decades‑long footprint nationwide. ICE records show that Sylvester Joseph, a key member, was sentenced to 63 months in prison for his role in a multi‑state conspiracy that bilked victims out of millions. Adams County District Attorney Eric Weiss praised the teamwork between local and federal agencies. “This arrest underscores how resourceful these criminals are and why cooperation is essential,” Weiss said in a statement. “Our office will pursue the strongest possible penalties under Pennsylvania law.” For Gettysburg mothers like the first victim—who asked to remain anonymous—the financial and emotional toll has been profound. “I feel violated knowing someone was driving around pretending to be me,” she told reporters. “I hope this case warns others to lock up their personal items.” Galicia was formally charged on July 14 with forgery, identity theft, theft by deception and receiving stolen property. She remains at large under a State Police warrant. Anyone with information on her whereabouts is urged to contact Adams County detectives or Crime Stoppers. Beyond the immediate arrests, local bankers say the case has prompted new security measures. ACNB recently announced plans to install additional cameras and require in‑branch ID verification for all drive‑through transactions—a policy change that lobbyists hope will deter future “Felony Lane” copycats.
